This week the National Diet opened Monday morning, 1/16/2017, to once again pick up the topic of whether or not Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution was still relevant or in need of major reform. Article 9, which is the clause that outlaws war as a means to settle international disputes involving the state and has been extremely controversial within Japan as growing tensions and globalization make the world a seemingly more dangerous place to live in. Specifically, the Article declares that Japan will not maintain a military force with which it could use in times of war, however Japan maintains a "Self Defense Force" with which they aim to keep the minimum amount of "security forces" by which to defend themselves from an outside force. The SDF also happens to be the 9th largest military in the world.

In recent years Japan's government has been witness to countless attempts to address the article, mostly to press for reinterpretations of the clause though a few pushes have been made to abolish it completely by leading political parties. In 2007 the Prime Minister called for a "Bold Review" of the article and in 2012 the National Diet supported a constitutional amendment to reduce or abolish restrictions imposed by Article 9. Only recently, in 2014 did Japan pass a reinterpretation of Article 9 which would allow Japan to exercise the right of "collective self defense" and exercise military action if one of its allies were to be attacked. The reinterpretation of Article 9 is a move that Japan's greatest ally, the Unites States, has been pushing for for quite some time.

The National Diet is meeting to determine whether or not the article is still needed or if it needs reforms.

Meaningful versions

When I started Cashmere, I didn't have a great understanding of software versioning. I've now decided on a versioning scheme that I think suits the nature of this project well. Shout-out to @j_ and @alphacys for the advice.

Cashmere now uses a date-based version number (year.month). This number will change when I add features, but not if I'm just fixing some minor bug. I think this is a good compromise between simple and informative. Well defined versions are useful, but some four-digit number would be overkill here. I may release two versions in one month, especially at the beginning, in which case it will be 15.8-2 or something.

New stuff

Icons are no longer hosted by Dropbox. This was a major issue that needed addressing. Dropbox has limits on both total bandwidth and HTTP requests, so if too many people accessed those files, Dropbox would stop hosting them. These files are now being hosted through Cashmere's github.io page (just a placeholder at the moment). Let me know if there are any problems with them, but from what I can tell they only have limits on individual file size and total repo size, not bandwidth.

Modal dialogs have been properly styled. These are the things that pop up like the login form or the one you get if you try to downvoat with less than 100CCP. They now match the style of Cashmere much better.

Selected text has been styled. This provides a more consistent look across different operating systems. If you aren't sure what I mean, go ahead and select some text on this page. I think it looks nicer. I have also provided variables for changing this in the _settings.scss file.

Other stuff. I can't list all the changes in this release because many things have been changed here and there in the 9 days since Cashmere was first published and depending on when a subverse started using Cashmere, a lot of these changes would not be new to anyone. This highlights the need for proper versioning. I will be able to provide better specifics with the next release.

Please update

If you're using Cashmere in your sub, it is highly recommended that you update to v15.8, especially because of the Dropbox issue.

 

I will make another post soon listing the issues and features to be addressed in the next release.

I think the thing that's most misunderstood about relativity is that you don't need an FTL engine to reach Alpha Centauri in 9 minutes. It's entirely possible to reach any place in the Universe in any arbitrarily short period of time if you've got a powerful enough conventional engine (and some way to resist the acceleration), but what you give up is that your place of origin and your destination will age much faster than you. So you can get to Alpha Centauri tomorrow, but that will be 'tomorrow' for you, not for Alpha Centauri or Earth.

That is enough to colonize any galaxy, but not to keep contact between the colonies.

You're neglecting to consider the "tyranny of the rocket equation", as Randall Munroe (author of XKCD) puts it. It's not just about having a powerful rocket engine, you need to consider the fuel. The more fuel you add to a rocket, the more fuel you need to get that extra weight moving. He nicely illustrates the difference in rocket mass needed to accelerate a rocket to a significant velocity in his short "what if" on retrieving the Voyager probe.

Right now our options for interstellar travel are:

1) Tiny probes on ordinary rockets that move comparatively slowly (Voyager left the solar system more than 35 years after launch, and it's at nowhere near relativistic velocity).

2) Impractically huge rockets to do what you described.

3) Fuel-efficient but incredibly low thrust (and therefore also slow) engines like ion drives.

Even if a drive isn't "true FTL", anything that breaks the above mould would be meaningful on a species-wide scale.

Oh, yes, we're not nearly close enough to powerful and efficient enough engines. I'm only saying we don't need faster-than-light to colonize the galaxy... close-to-light is almost just as good.

From the point we're at now, we still need some super-efficient, cosmic-gas-breathing engine, or some anti-matter fuel for maximum energy density. There'd also be a very very serious problem with ablation from cosmic radiation and particles at relativistic speeds. So throw in some amazing shield technology to the requirements list.
